draft.title: Squatters and the wool industry
card: Squatters were settlers who moved their sheep onto huge areas of land beyond the official limits of settlement. At first they had no legal right to the land.
Sheep farming suited the colonies. Wool was light and worth a lot for its weight, so it could be carried over long distances and shipped to British mills.
By the mid 1800s wool was the colonies' main export. The money it earned helped the colonies grow.

Squatters needed fresh grass and water for their flocks, so they kept moving further inland. Settlement spread with them. The land they used was already home to First Nations peoples, who lost access to it.
draft.remember: Wool earned the colonies' export income, and the search for grazing land pushed settlement inland.

a.q: Why did the wool industry push settlement further inland?
opts: Large flocks needed fresh grass and water, so squatters moved out
Wool mills were built in the inland districts
The government ordered all farmers to move inland
Wool could not be shipped from coastal towns
a.why: Large flocks needed fresh grass and water, so squatters kept looking for new land away from the coast. The mills were in Britain, so mills inland were not the reason.
a.clue: Think about what a large flock needs to eat and drink.

b.q: In the 1840s Tom takes his flock of 3000 sheep onto land far from the nearest town, without any legal right to it. What is Tom?
opts: A squatter
A convict
A gold miner
A free trader
b.why: A squatter was a settler who grazed sheep on large areas of land beyond the official limits, with no legal right at first. Tom's actions match this. Nothing in the case suggests mining or trade.
b.clue: Look at what Tom does with the land.
